title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input Sanitization and Deterministic Verification
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) that measured whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used the declared generator gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within an orchestration adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: Baseline 135/141 (95.7447%); Guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. We reconcile preregistration wording vs the formal estimand, document pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate reuse, disclose a protocol deviation (unset runtime sampling temperature), and discuss operational interpretation and limitations constrained by synthetic scope and single-model/validator evaluation. All principal numeric claims are supported by the archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest [14]).

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed to translate high-level operator intent into device CLI to reduce manual NetOps workload, but they can produce syntactic mistakes, incorrect ordering, and other deployment-relevant errors. Deterministic validators that encode explicit configuration and safety invariants (e.g., CLI grammar, required sequencing, protected-interface rules) are practical gates for deployment because they accept or reject candidates based on semantic properties rather than string similarity [5–7]. Prior prototype work demonstrates that coupling LLMs with validators and constrained repair improves outcome metrics on narrow tasks, but published evaluations often measure token or reference overlap rather than deployability as judged by a verifier [3,8,9].

This paper reports a narrowly scoped, preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment asking: Does template-based input sanitization together with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair change the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents? The preregistration defined a single formal estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) and registered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics so that each paired comparison isolates downstream guarded-pipeline effects (sanitization, gating, and bounded repair) applied to one shared LLM draft per intent. We executed the registered pipeline end-to-end and present confirmatory inference, diagnostics linking repairs to discordant outcomes, sensitivity accounting for preregistered missingness rules, and interpretations bounded by the synthetic scope and single-model/validator design.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic network-verification tools such as Header Space Analysis and VeriFlow enable rapid, model-based checks of forwarding, access-control, and sequencing invariants and therefore can be used as deployment gates that report property-level violations rather than surface differences [5–7]. Their representational focus makes them suitable validators for LLM-assisted automation but also limits coverage: protocol-level dynamics and some runtime semantics are not automatically captured. Empirical evaluations of LLMs for NetOps (e.g., NetConfEval, NetLLMBench) report that model-only generation frequently produces syntactic errors and higher-level semantic mistakes (ordering, precondition violations, protected-interface breaches), motivating generate–validate–repair architectures that integrate verifier feedback into constrained repair steps [3,8,9].

Security research on LLM-integrated systems documents prompt-injection and indirect prompt attacks that can subvert agentic pipelines when untrusted inputs are incorporated without sanitization; this motivates operational defenses such as template-based input sanitization, slot validation, and deterministic gating policies [10, Not What You've Signed Up For]. Prior prototype demonstrations of generate–validate–repair approaches show measurable improvements but remain limited in scale and diversity and therefore do not establish production-ready reliability across vendors, protocols, and large topologies [11,3]. Our work situates itself by preregistering an estimand that uses deterministic-validator acceptance as the primary quantity of interest and by executing an artifact-backed paired design that preserves shared_initial_candidate semantics so that observed paired differences are attributable to downstream sanitization, gating, and bounded repair.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and formal estimand. Study cand-2026-03 was preregistered prior to observing outcomes. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: for each adversarial intent (paired unit) define a binary outcome equal to 1 if the deterministic validator would accept the final candidate for deployment and 0 otherwise. The confirmatory test specified in the preregistration is an exact two-sided McNemar on paired outcomes; confidence intervals are bootstrap percentile intervals with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729.

Design, task bank, and adversary model. The preregistered design targeted 150 adversarial intents (paired episodes across Baseline and Guarded). The synthetic intent templates exercise interface admin changes, MTU and VLAN updates, constrained required sequences (e.g., shutdown–change–restore), and protected-interface rules. The adversary model deterministically mutated templates (string-level and slot mutations); generation seeds and the mutation taxonomy are archived in the execution manifest. Scope is explicitly synthetic and limited to the deterministic CLI grammar encoded in the validator.

Model, validator, orchestration, and declared configuration. The declared generator is gpt-5-mini and the deterministic validator is deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 generate–validate–repair adapter implementing the guarded pipeline. The archived model configuration records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset); we disclose this unset parameter as a protocol deviation because provider-side defaults can affect sampling determinism.

Pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate. The preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate. For each paired intent the pipeline executed a single initial LLM call producing the shared_initial_candidate used for both Baseline and Guarded scoring. Baseline scoring applied the deterministic validator directly to that candidate. The Guarded branch first applied template-based sanitization and a deterministic gating policy; if the sanitizer/gate allowed, at-most-one automated repair LLM call was permitted. The validator then re-evaluated the sanitized or repaired candidate and recorded the final guarded decision. Provider-call accounting and stage counts (shared_initial_generation events and repair-stage events) are available in the archived reconciliation artifacts and deterministic reconciliation.

Missingness, exclusions, and analysis. The preregistered missingness plan excluded a paired unit only when both paired runs were technical failures (model API failure, verifier timeout, or parser error). The execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 282, failed_episode_count = 18, and complete_pair_count = 141 after applying the exclusion rule. Primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 implementing exact two-sided McNemar and the bootstrap CI procedure above. All analysis parameters, seeds, resample counts, and numeric outputs are archived and reproducible from the execution and analysis artifacts referenced in the execution manifest [14].
sections.results:
Execution and provider-call accounting. The run completed 282 of 300 planned episodes; 18 episodes failed for technical reasons per the preregistered missingness rules and were handled by the preregistered exclusion rule (exclude pair only when both runs failed). Provider-call accounting in the deterministic reconciliation shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 156, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 147, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 9, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 6. Complete_pair_count entering primary analysis = 141.

Condition-level and paired outcomes. Condition summaries used by the primary analysis were baseline_successes = 135/141 (baseline success rate = 0.9574468085106383) and guarded_successes = 141/141 (guarded success rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table observed n11 = 135 (both accepted), n10 = 6 (guarded accepted, baseline rejected), n01 = 0 (baseline accepted, guarded rejected), n00 = 0 (both rejected). The preregistered exact two-sided McNemar test yields p = 0.03125. The paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. These quantities appear in the archived confirmatory_results and analysis artifacts cited in the execution manifest [14].

Discordant-case diagnostics and repair association. The six discordant pairs (n10) are traceable in the archived per-episode validator traces. Deterministic reconciliation links repair-stage activity to these discordant pairs: stage_counts.reported repair = 6 and each discordant pair's validator trace indicates sanitizer normalization and/or a single permitted repair converted a draft that the baseline validator rejected into a final candidate the validator accepted. Per-episode traces retained in the archive document final_configuration, validation_before/after, and repair_applied flags.

Sensitivity to technical failures. Nine paired units were excluded because both runs failed technically. As a conservative, non-preregistered sensitivity check treating those excluded pairs as failures yields baseline acceptance = 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded acceptance = 141/150 = 0.9400. This conservative recalculation illustrates the dependence of marginal rates on handling of technical failures but does not alter the primary paired inference which uses the preregistered exclusion rule and complete_pairs = 141.

Unexecuted preregistered items. The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and the false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed in this run; consequently no empirical false-positive-blocking rates are reported and this omission constrains operational conclusions about false-positive blocking.
sections.discussion:
Estimand interpretation and preregistration reconciliation. The preregistration natural-language hypothesis framed the expected effect as verifier-gating reducing attacker success, but the registered formal estimand measured paired validator acceptance-for-deployment (guarded − baseline). These differ: an increase in validator acceptance can reflect successful repair of reparable but benign drafts rather than reduced attacker success. Our observed guarded→higher acceptance (≈0.04255 absolute increase) occurred because sanitizer normalization and permitted single repairs recovered drafts that the baseline validator rejected. Therefore the preregistered directional attacker-centric claim is not supported under an attacker-centric interpretation; we report and interpret results with respect to the archived formal estimand and explicitly caution against equating validator acceptance with attacker-centric safety without an independent semantic-safety oracle.

Operational implications and repair–gate co-design. In this synthetic setting, template-based input sanitization combined with a bounded repair policy reduced the frequency of drafts rejected by the validator by recovering reparable drafts, potentially reducing operator rework. However, repairs that enable acceptance can be risky if they alter intended semantics or mask adversarial manipulations. The six discordant cases illustrate that repairs were causally associated with moved-into-acceptance outcomes; operational deployment therefore requires co-design: specify gating policies, repair scope, and validator expressiveness jointly and include independent semantic-safety checks before automated acceptance in high-assurance settings.

Threats to validity and generalization. Internal validity: technical failures (18/300) reduced effective sample size; the preregistered exclusion rule was applied. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes CLI grammar, sequencing, and specified invariants but does not capture all protocol-level or runtime dynamics; acceptance-for-deployment is therefore a partial proxy for operational safety. External validity: the experiment used a single declared generator (gpt-5-mini), a single validator implementation, and a synthetic adversarial intent bank, limiting generalization across vendors, CLI dialects, and production traffic. Conclusion validity: the observed absolute effect was small against a high baseline (ceiling effect); statistical significance (p = 0.03125) indicates detectability under the paired design but not necessarily broad practical impact.

Reproducibility, protocol deviation, and recommended deterministic reproduction. The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset), which we disclose as a protocol deviation because provider-side defaults may affect sampling. To preserve paired comparability despite the unset parameter the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single generation per pair). For deterministic reproduction we recommend explicitly setting temperature = 0 and re-executing the archived execution manifest; the manifest, reconciliation artifacts (provider_call audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 156, completed = 147, failed = 9, shared_initial_generation = 150, repair = 6), and analysis artifacts contain the run record needed for verification [14].

Recommendations for future work. (1) Execute the preregistered benign-control to measure false-positive blocking and report the preregistered secondary estimand; (2) preregister attacker-centric estimands that couple validator acceptance with an independent semantic-safety oracle or reachability tests; (3) diversify generators and validators across vendors and CLI dialects to assess external generalization; (4) fix sampling settings (temperature = 0) for deterministic reproduction; and (5) consider restricting automatic repairs to semantics-preserving transformations verified by independent checks. Each recommendation follows from the archived artifact evidence and provider-call accounting in the execution manifest [14].
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]; bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Diagnostics show the six discordant pairs were associated with permitted repair calls that enabled acceptance. Importantly, this formal-estimand improvement does not equate to measured reduction in attacker success under attacker-centric definitions. The run is limited by synthetic scope, a single declared model/validator, and a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). Future work should execute the preregistered benign-control, measure attacker-centric estimands with independent semantic-safety oracles, diversify models/validators, and set explicit sampling parameters for reproducible deterministic runs. All principal numbers and reconciliation claims above are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts; the execution manifest is the primary machine-verifiable archive and is cited here as [14].

limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
